articles.title: CRISPR is now being used to control genes, not just edit them
articles.summary: CRISPR-based treatments that work by turning genes on or off are being tested in trials, and could be even more powerful than conventional gene editing
articles.content:
CRISPR-based treatments that work by turning genes on or off are being tested in trials, and could be even more powerful than conventional gene editing

A transmission electron micrograph of hepatitis B viral particles, an infection for which the new approach to CRISPR is showing promise Imago/Alamy

Gene editing is already saving lives, with hundreds of trials happening around the world. But there is an upstart in the wings: epigenome editing, which turns genes on or off instead of altering them. The first human trials of epigenome editing are producing promising results, and it could prove to be an extremely powerful tool.

“What’s great is that we now have a demonstration of epigenome editing in the clinic showing that it’s effective at what it’s supposed to do,” Charles Gersbach at Duke University in North Carolina told the Engineering the Epigenome conference in Paris earlier in November.

Epigenome editing has tremendous potential for treating a wide range of conditions. It could also help in a less direct way, said Gersbach, by helping biologists understand our genome and thus work out the root causes of common conditions.

Advertisement

“We don’t really know what the cause is of most of our common, most debilitating diseases,” said Gersbach. “It is not surprising that we don’t know what causes Alzheimer’s or neuropsychiatric conditions or autoimmune disease when we don’t know what the vast majority of our genome does.”

Gersbach is a cofounder of Tune Therapeutics, one of several companies testing epigenome editing as a treatment for the hepatitis B virus that infects the liver. Globally, around 240 million people were infected with hepatitis B as of 2024, and the virus could eventually kill many of them by causing liver failure or cancer.

Vaccines can prevent hepatitis B, but we don’t have good treatments. The problem is that our immune system can’t completely get rid of hepatitis B because the virus can hide indefinitely, in the form of circular loops of viral DNA inside liver cells. Viral DNA also integrates into the genome of liver cells, which is why the virus can cause cancer. “Each cell could have dozens of copies of this viral genome,” said Gersbach.

Using standard CRISPR gene editing to destroy the viral DNA would be risky. Making lots of DNA cuts at the same time increases the risk of the wrong ends being joined together, which could cause chromosomal abnormalities and even cancer.

But what if the viral DNA could be permanently deactivated without having to cut it? That’s what epigenetic editing can do.

Cells naturally make so-called epigenetic changes to their DNA to control gene activity. For instance, as cells specialise into muscle or nerve cells, some genes need to be turned on, and others turned off.

There are many kinds of epigenetic changes, but they can all be thought of as labels that tell cells whether a particular piece of DNA should be active. For instance, attaching methyl tags to DNA – a process called methylation – can shut down genes without altering the underlying sequence.

Standard CRISPR gene editing relies on a protein called Cas9, which has two key components: a targeting part that finds a specific piece of DNA, and the “scissors” that cut DNA at that spot. Replace the scissors with an enzyme that adds methyl tags, say, and the modified CRISPR Cas9 can be used to make epigenetic changes. In other words, a gene editor can be modified into an epigenome editor.

Early attempts at this worked, but the gene-silencing effect lasted only a few days, said Angelo Lombardo at San Raffaele University in Italy. “That was a big problem, at least for therapy applications,” said Lombardo. “You want an epigenetic editor that can impose stable gene silencing.”

His team succeeded in making one by linking parts of three different enzymes to a de-scissored CRISPR Cas9 protein. Animal studies have shown that these kinds of editors can permanently shut down gene activity, with the effect passed on when cells divide, just like most natural methylation.

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

It’s working in people, too, said Gersbach. In the Tune trial, researchers have been measuring levels of an RNA molecule produced only when the hepatitis B genome is active. “At high doses, or with multi-dosing, we’re getting 97 to 99 per cent repression,” he said.

The effect also persists after just a single treatment, and there have been no serious safety issues. It remains to be seen whether this will prevent liver damage and cancer, but for the wider field, what matters is that it is working in the sense of shutting down genes inside the human body.

“Epigenetic editing is on par even with CRISPR gene knockout. It is maintained, and it is reversible,” said Marianne Rots at the University Medical Center Groningen in the Netherlands.

In other words, epigenetic editing can do everything standard CRISPR Cas9 gene editing can do but without the risks of cutting DNA. What it can’t do is correct disease-causing mutations, unlike more advanced forms of CRISPR gene editing, such as base editing and prime editing.

But controlling gene activity alone could help treat a huge range of conditions, including inherited ones. Gersbach points out that the first approved CRISPR Cas9 treatment, for sickle cell disease, works by destroying the “off switch” for the gene for fetal hemoglobin, not by correcting mutations. Epigenome editors should be able to achieve the same result.

Another treatment being tested in people lowers cholesterol by using CRISPR base editing to wreck the “on switch” for a gene called PSK9. Lombardo’s team has developed an epigenome editor that achieves the same result. In monkeys, it reduced PSK9 activity by 90 per cent, resulting in a 70 per cent fall in cholesterol. In theory at least, the epigenome-editing version should be safer.

But epigenome editing does have drawbacks. As several speakers at the conference described, the complexities of how cells control gene activity mean an epigenome editor that works beautifully for shutting down one gene may fail to turn off another gene, or may work in some cell types but not in others. “It depends on the context,” says Stylianos Tsagkris at the European Molecular Biology Laboratory (EMBL) in Rome.

Tsagkris has developed a way of targeting thousands of sites in a single study to assess how well different epigenome editors work. The ultimate aim is to predict which epigenome editors will work in which circumstances, but there’s a long way to go, he says.

Another issue for the field is that, while existing epigenetic editors work well for some genes, at least, they could do with improvement. For instance, editors that consist of a de-scissored CRISPR Cas9 fused to other enzymes are very large proteins, making them hard to deliver, said RJ Jiao at Rice University in Houston, Texas. Some can be harmful to cells, too.

So his team has used an AI system called AlphaFold to design an epigenome editor where the de-scissored Cas9 isn’t fused to enzymes, but instead binds to existing ones in a cell to achieve the same results. This approach was inspired by the way many natural proteins form complexes, Jiao told the conference.

Our ability to design new proteins like this is rapidly advancing, he said. “The same approach can likely be applied to many other epigenome-modifying proteins.”

Then there’s delivery – getting epigenome editors into the organs where they are needed. At the moment, only the liver is easily targetable, hence the hepatitis B trials. But this delivery problem isn’t specific to epigenome editing, and many groups and companies are making progress towards targeting other organs.

The big one is the brain. Turning genes on or off there could help treat everything from mental illnesses and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s to even multiple sclerosis. “Ninety per cent of the interesting targets are in the brain, so when we can target that, the field will really take off,” says Jamie Hackett at EMBL.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant advancement in gene therapy using epigenome editing with CRISPR technology, which can turn genes on or off without cutting DNA, reducing risks associated with traditional gene editing. This new approach is already showing promising results in human trials for hepatitis B, a disease affecting millions globally, and holds potential for treating a wide range of conditions including neurodegenerative and inherited diseases. The story has broad significance for public health, provides detailed scientific context, and highlights ongoing progress and future potential, meeting all criteria for inspiring good news.
articles.personality_title: New CRISPR method controls genes safely in human trials
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have been using CRISPR technology to edit genes by cutting DNA. This method helps treat diseases but carries risks because cutting DNA can cause mistakes. Now, researchers are testing a new way called epigenome editing, which turns genes on or off without cutting DNA.

**What happened** – For the first time, epigenome editing is being tested in human trials. A company called Tune Therapeutics is using this method to treat hepatitis B, a virus that infects the liver and affects about 240 million people worldwide. Instead of cutting the viral DNA, the new CRISPR tool adds chemical tags that switch off the virus permanently. Early results show 97 to 99 percent success in stopping the virus from being active, and the effect lasts a long time after just one treatment.

**Impact** – This new approach is important because it avoids the risks of cutting DNA, such as unwanted changes that could cause cancer. It also works in a reversible way, meaning genes can be turned back on if needed. Besides hepatitis B, this method could help treat many diseases, including inherited disorders, high cholesterol, and brain conditions like Alzheimer’s. It also helps scientists understand how genes work by controlling their activity precisely.

**What's next step** – Researchers are working to improve this technology to target more organs beyond the liver, especially the brain, which is linked to many diseases. They are also using artificial intelligence to design better CRISPR tools that are smaller and safer. More human trials will test how well epigenome editing can treat different diseases over time.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A safer CRISPR method that turns genes on or off without cutting DNA is showing strong promise in human trials, opening new paths to treat many diseases.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle méthode CRISPR contrôle les gènes en toute sécurité lors d'essais humains
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques utilisent la technologie CRISPR pour modifier les gènes en coupant l’ADN. Cette méthode aide à traiter des maladies mais comporte des risques car couper l’ADN peut provoquer des erreurs. Aujourd’hui, des chercheurs testent une nouvelle méthode appelée édition de l’épigénome, qui active ou désactive les gènes sans couper l’ADN.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Pour la première fois, l’édition de l’épigénome est testée chez l’humain. Une entreprise nommée Tune Therapeutics utilise cette méthode pour traiter l’hépatite B, un virus qui infecte le foie et touche environ 240 millions de personnes dans le monde. Au lieu de couper l’ADN viral, le nouvel outil CRISPR ajoute des marques chimiques qui désactivent le virus de façon permanente. Les premiers résultats montrent un succès de 97 à 99 % pour arrêter l’activité du virus, et l’effet dure longtemps après un seul traitement.

**Impact** – Cette nouvelle approche est importante car elle évite les risques liés à la coupure de l’ADN, comme des changements indésirables pouvant causer un cancer. Elle fonctionne aussi de façon réversible, ce qui signifie que les gènes peuvent être réactivés si besoin. En plus de l’hépatite B, cette méthode pourrait aider à traiter de nombreuses maladies, y compris des troubles héréditaires, un cholestérol élevé et des maladies cérébrales comme Alzheimer. Elle aide aussi les scientifiques à mieux comprendre le fonctionnement des gènes en contrôlant précisément leur activité.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs travaillent à améliorer cette technologie pour cibler d’autres organes que le foie, en particulier le cerveau, lié à beaucoup de maladies. Ils utilisent aussi l’intelligence artificielle pour concevoir des outils CRISPR plus petits et plus sûrs. D’autres essais humains testeront l’efficacité de l’édition de l’épigénome sur différentes maladies à long terme.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Une méthode CRISPR plus sûre qui active ou désactive les gènes sans couper l’ADN montre de très bons résultats dans des essais humains, ouvrant de nouvelles voies pour traiter de nombreuses maladies.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo método CRISPR controla genes con seguridad en ensayos humanos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han estado usando la tecnología CRISPR para editar genes cortando el ADN. Este método ayuda a tratar enfermedades pero tiene riesgos porque cortar el ADN puede causar errores. Ahora, los investigadores prueban una nueva forma llamada edición del epigenoma, que enciende o apaga genes sin cortar el ADN.

**Qué pasó** – Por primera vez, la edición del epigenoma se está probando en ensayos humanos. Una empresa llamada Tune Therapeutics usa este método para tratar la hepatitis B, un virus que infecta el hígado y afecta a unos 240 millones de personas en el mundo. En lugar de cortar el ADN viral, la nueva herramienta CRISPR agrega etiquetas químicas que apagan el virus de forma permanente. Los primeros resultados muestran entre 97 y 99 por ciento de éxito para detener la actividad del virus, y el efecto dura mucho tiempo después de un solo tratamiento.

**Impacto** – Este nuevo enfoque es importante porque evita los riesgos de cortar el ADN, como cambios no deseados que podrían causar cáncer. Además, funciona de manera reversible, lo que significa que los genes se pueden volver a activar si es necesario. Aparte de la hepatitis B, este método podría ayudar a tratar muchas enfermedades, incluyendo trastornos hereditarios, colesterol alto y enfermedades cerebrales como el Alzheimer. También ayuda a los científicos a entender mejor cómo funcionan los genes controlando su actividad con precisión.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores trabajan para mejorar esta tecnología y poder dirigirla a más órganos además del hígado, especialmente al cerebro, que está relacionado con muchas enfermedades. También usan inteligencia artificial para diseñar mejores herramientas CRISPR que sean más pequeñas y seguras. Más ensayos humanos probarán qué tan bien puede tratar la edición del epigenoma diferentes enfermedades a largo plazo.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Un método CRISPR más seguro que enciende o apaga genes sin cortar el ADN muestra gran potencial en ensayos humanos, abriendo nuevas formas de tratar muchas enfermedades.

articles.title: Vagus nerve stimulation slows growth and spread of pancreatic cancer
articles.summary: An electrical implant around the oesophagus that stimulates the vagus nerve improved outcomes in mice with pancreatic cancer by making their tumours more susceptible to immunotherapy
articles.content:
An electrical implant around the oesophagus that stimulates the vagus nerve improved outcomes in mice with pancreatic cancer by making their tumours more susceptible to immunotherapy

Pancreatic cancer is typically very difficult to treat CENTRE JEAN-PERRIN/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY

An electrical implant that stimulates the vagus nerve slowed the growth and spread of pancreatic tumours in mice. The approach seems to work by helping cancer-killing immune cells infiltrate tumours, enabling a treatment that doesn’t normally work for pancreatic cancer to become effective.

“It’s very exciting,” says Timothy Wang at Columbia University in New York, who wasn’t involved in the research. “It’s the first study I know where electrical manipulation has been used to treat tumours outside the brain.”

The intervention made the tumours susceptible to immunotherapy, which helps immune cells destroy cancer but usually fails against pancreatic tumours. “That could be very significant for patients,” says Wang. “Getting immunotherapy to work is the holy grail right now for pancreatic cancer. It’s thought to be key to long-term survival.”

Advertisement

One way to potentially make immunotherapy work is through electrical stimulation. This is already used to treat some kinds of brain cancer, such as glioblastoma. Now, Lu Gan at the Huazhong University of Science and Technology in China and their colleagues have tested it for pancreatic cancer. More than 500,000 people are diagnosed with pancreatic cancer a year, of whom only 13 per cent survive 5 years, making it one of the deadliest forms of cancer.

Prior research by Wang and his colleagues has also shown that blocking electrical signals in the vagus nerve, which connects the brain to other organs, increases the growth of pancreatic cancer in mice. To see whether stimulating the nerve has the reverse effect, Gan’s team developed an electrical device – roughly 1-centimetre long – that wraps around part of the oesophagus.

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

When activated by ultrasound waves, sent from outside the body, the device sends electrical signals along a branch of the vagus nerve that runs from the oesophagus to the pancreas.

To put it to the test, the researchers implanted the device, which wasn’t yet activated, into mice. Six days later, cancerous cells were injected into their pancreas. After tumours had formed, the team activated the device for 20 minutes a day in half the mice. It remained inactive in the remaining mice, acting as a control.

About two weeks later, the tumours in the control mice weighed about 230 milligrams, on average, compared with about 190 milligrams in the mice that received electrical stimulation – an almost 20 per cent difference. “I don’t think anyone would have predicted that big an effect,” says Wang.

The pancreatic cancer cells had also spread to more than 10 other parts of the control mice’s bodies, on average – about double the degree of spread that occurred among those that received electrical stimulation.

The more tumours spread, the deadlier they tend to be, however, the researchers didn’t measure the mice’s survival outcomes. This is probably because that would involve tracking a large number of mice over a longer period, and this was just a proof-of-concept study, says Wang. The researchers did find, however, that the device had no known short-term safety issues.

In another part of the experiment, the researchers found that the electrical stimulation seemed to boost the number of cancer-killing immune cells, called T-cells and natural killer cells, in the tumours. It also reduced the abundance of other kinds of immune cells, called MDSCs, which suppress T-cells.

Exactly how this occurred is unclear, but prior studies suggest that stimulating the vagus nerve increases the release of a neurotransmitter called acetylcholine, which can bind to receptors on the surface of immune and cancer cells, altering their behaviour, says Wang.

Finally, the team explored whether the approach could make pancreatic tumours respond to an immunotherapy drug, called anti-PD1, which activates T-cells but is usually ineffective against this type of cancer. “Pancreatic cancer is notorious for having an almost zero response to immunotherapy, and most believe that’s because pancreatic cancer has a tremendously fibrous structure, which stops immune cells getting in,” says Wang. If electrical stimulation allows T-cells to infiltrate the pancreas, immunotherapy stands a better chance, he says.

The researchers found that anti-PD1 alone had no substantial effect on tumour growth in mice with pancreatic tumours. But combining it with electrical stimulation slowed tumour growth and stopped cancers spreading more than electrical stimulation alone.

This suggests this combination treatment could improve survival outcomes, says Wang. “Long-term survival in pancreatic cancer really does require T-cell immunity and getting immunotherapy to work.” It may be even more effective when combined with a non-immunotherapy drug, called daraxonrasib, that roughly doubles survival time in people with pancreatic cancer, says Wang.

Further research should first test whether the findings can be replicated in other mouse models of pancreatic cancer that better mimic what happens in people, for instance, by using mice that have been genetically engineered to develop pancreatic tumours, says Wang. These studies could also assess survival outcomes, he says. If successful, trials in people could start within the next couple of years, he says.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in pancreatic cancer treatment using electrical stimulation of the vagus nerve, which slowed tumor growth and spread in mice and enhanced immunotherapy effectiveness. Pancreatic cancer is a deadly disease with low survival rates, so this advancement has broad potential impact on patient outcomes globally. The study is detailed and focused on a single promising treatment approach with clear positive implications for future human trials.
articles.personality_title: Electrical nerve stimulation slows pancreatic cancer growth in mice
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Pancreatic cancer is one of the deadliest cancers, with only about 13% of patients surviving five years. It is very hard to treat because the cancer resists most therapies, including immunotherapy, which helps the immune system fight cancer.

**What happened** – Scientists in China tested a small electrical device that wraps around the oesophagus and stimulates the vagus nerve, which connects the brain to the pancreas. They implanted this device in mice and used ultrasound waves to activate it daily. Mice with the device turned on had tumors that grew slower and spread less compared to mice without stimulation. The device also helped immune cells enter the tumors, making immunotherapy drugs effective when they normally wouldn’t be.

**Impact** – This is the first time electrical stimulation of the vagus nerve has been shown to slow cancer growth outside the brain. By helping immune cells reach pancreatic tumors, this method could make immunotherapy work for a cancer that is usually resistant. This approach may lead to better treatments and longer survival for patients with pancreatic cancer.

**What's next step** – Researchers want to test this device in other mouse models that are closer to human disease and measure how it affects survival. If these studies go well, clinical trials in people could start in a few years to see if the treatment works safely and effectively in patients.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Stimulating the vagus nerve with an electrical implant slowed pancreatic tumor growth and helped immunotherapy work in mice, offering hope for new treatments against this tough cancer.
articles.personality_title_fr: La stimulation électrique du nerf vague ralentit la croissance du cancer du pancréas chez la souris
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le cancer du pancréas est l’un des cancers les plus mortels, avec seulement environ 13 % de survie à cinq ans. Il est très difficile à traiter car il résiste à la plupart des thérapies, y compris l’immunothérapie, qui aide le système immunitaire à combattre le cancer.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs en Chine ont testé un petit dispositif électrique qui s’enroule autour de l’œsophage et stimule le nerf vague, qui relie le cerveau au pancréas. Ils ont implanté ce dispositif chez des souris et l’ont activé chaque jour avec des ondes ultrasonores. Les souris avec le dispositif activé avaient des tumeurs qui poussaient plus lentement et se propageaient moins que celles sans stimulation. Le dispositif a aussi aidé les cellules immunitaires à pénétrer dans les tumeurs, rendant l’immunothérapie efficace alors qu’elle ne l’était pas d’habitude.

**Impact** – C’est la première fois que la stimulation électrique du nerf vague ralentit la croissance d’un cancer en dehors du cerveau. En aidant les cellules immunitaires à atteindre les tumeurs du pancréas, cette méthode pourrait rendre l’immunothérapie efficace contre un cancer habituellement résistant. Cette approche pourrait améliorer les traitements et la survie des patients.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent tester ce dispositif sur d’autres modèles de souris plus proches de la maladie humaine et mesurer l’effet sur la survie. Si ces essais sont concluants, des essais cliniques chez l’humain pourraient commencer dans quelques années pour vérifier la sécurité et l’efficacité.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La stimulation du nerf vague par un implant électrique a ralenti la croissance des tumeurs du pancréas et rendu l’immunothérapie efficace chez la souris, ouvrant la voie à de nouveaux traitements contre ce cancer difficile.
articles.personality_title_es: La estimulación eléctrica del nervio vago ralentiza el crecimiento del cáncer de páncreas en ratones
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El cáncer de páncreas es uno de los más mortales, con solo un 13 % de supervivencia a cinco años. Es muy difícil de tratar porque no responde bien a la mayoría de los tratamientos, incluida la inmunoterapia, que ayuda al sistema inmunitario a combatir el cáncer.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos en China probaron un pequeño dispositivo eléctrico que se coloca alrededor del esófago y estimula el nervio vago, que conecta el cerebro con el páncreas. Implantaron este dispositivo en ratones y lo activaron diariamente con ondas de ultrasonido. Los ratones con el dispositivo activado tuvieron tumores que crecieron más lento y se propagaron menos que los que no lo tenían activado. El dispositivo también ayudó a que las células inmunitarias entraran en los tumores, haciendo que la inmunoterapia funcionara cuando normalmente no lo hace.

**Impacto** – Es la primera vez que se muestra que la estimulación eléctrica del nervio vago puede frenar el crecimiento de cáncer fuera del cerebro. Al ayudar a las células inmunitarias a llegar a los tumores pancreáticos, este método podría hacer que la inmunoterapia funcione en un cáncer que suele ser resistente. Esto podría mejorar los tratamientos y aumentar la supervivencia de los pacientes.

**Próximos pasos** – Los investigadores quieren probar este dispositivo en otros modelos de ratones que imiten mejor la enfermedad humana y medir cómo afecta la supervivencia. Si estos estudios son positivos, podrían comenzar ensayos clínicos en humanos en unos años para ver si el tratamiento es seguro y efectivo.

**Resumen en una frase** – Estimular el nervio vago con un implante eléctrico ralentizó el crecimiento de tumores pancreáticos y ayudó a que la inmunoterapia funcionara en ratones, ofreciendo una nueva esperanza para tratar este cáncer difícil.

articles.title: Pharmacies get new powers to swap prescriptions during shortages
articles.summary: If a medicine is out of stock, staff can offer the same drug in a different strength or form, like a capsule instead of a pill.
articles.content:
Pharmacies are being given more freedom over the prescription medicines they can give to patients when items are out of stock.

Staff will be able to offer the same drug in a different strength or form – two 5mg tablets in the place of a 10mg pill, or a cream instead of an ointment, for example.

The change should help patients avoid repeat trips to their GP for an alternative prescription when the issue can be resolved safely and easily at the chemist.

And for the first time, children in England who miss their flu vaccination at school will be able to receive it at a pharmacy instead.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a policy change allowing pharmacies to substitute prescription medicines during shortages, improving patient access and convenience, and expanding flu vaccination options for children. This has a positive real-world impact on public health and benefits a broad population by reducing delays and healthcare visits.
articles.personality_title: Pharmacies can now swap medicines during shortages to help patients faster
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Sometimes, the medicines people need are not available at pharmacies because they are out of stock. This can cause delays and extra visits to the doctor to get new prescriptions.

**What happened** – Pharmacies in England have been given new powers to offer patients the same medicine but in a different strength or form if the original one is unavailable. For example, if a 10mg pill is out of stock, pharmacists can give two 5mg tablets instead. They can also switch between forms, like giving a cream instead of an ointment. Additionally, children who miss their flu shot at school can now get vaccinated at a pharmacy.

**Impact** – This change helps people get their medicines more quickly and easily, without needing to visit a doctor again for a new prescription. It also makes it simpler for children to get flu vaccinations, which can protect more families from illness. By allowing pharmacists to make these safe changes, patients save time and avoid extra trips.

**What's next step** – Pharmacies will start using these new powers right away, and health officials will watch to make sure the changes are safe and helpful. This could lead to more ways for pharmacists to support patients in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New rules let pharmacists safely swap medicines during shortages and offer flu vaccines to children missed at school, making healthcare quicker and easier.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les pharmacies peuvent maintenant échanger des médicaments en cas de pénurie pour aider les patients plus rapidement
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Parfois, les médicaments dont les patients ont besoin ne sont pas disponibles en pharmacie à cause des ruptures de stock. Cela peut entraîner des retards et des visites supplémentaires chez le médecin pour obtenir une nouvelle ordonnance.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Les pharmacies en Angleterre ont reçu de nouveaux pouvoirs pour proposer aux patients le même médicament, mais sous une autre dose ou forme, si celui d’origine est en rupture. Par exemple, si un comprimé de 10 mg manque, le pharmacien peut donner deux comprimés de 5 mg. Ils peuvent aussi changer la forme, comme proposer une crème au lieu d’une pommade. De plus, les enfants qui ont raté leur vaccin contre la grippe à l’école peuvent désormais se faire vacciner en pharmacie.

**Impact** – Ce changement aide les patients à obtenir leurs médicaments plus rapidement et plus facilement, sans devoir retourner chez le médecin pour une nouvelle ordonnance. Il facilite aussi la vaccination des enfants, ce qui protège davantage de familles contre la maladie. En permettant aux pharmaciens de faire ces changements en toute sécurité, les patients gagnent du temps et évitent des déplacements inutiles.

**Prochaine étape** – Les pharmacies vont commencer à utiliser ces nouveaux pouvoirs immédiatement, et les autorités sanitaires surveilleront pour s’assurer que les changements sont sûrs et utiles. Cela pourrait ouvrir la voie à plus de soutien des pharmaciens pour les patients à l’avenir.

**Une phrase clé** – De nouvelles règles permettent aux pharmaciens d’échanger des médicaments en cas de pénurie et d’offrir des vaccins contre la grippe aux enfants absents à l’école, rendant les soins de santé plus rapides et plus simples.
articles.personality_title_es: Las farmacias pueden ahora cambiar medicamentos durante escasez para ayudar a los pacientes más rápido
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – A veces, los medicamentos que necesitan las personas no están disponibles en las farmacias porque están agotados. Esto puede causar retrasos y visitas extras al médico para obtener nuevas recetas.

**Qué pasó** – Las farmacias en Inglaterra han recibido nuevos poderes para ofrecer a los pacientes el mismo medicamento pero en una dosis o forma diferente si el original no está disponible. Por ejemplo, si falta una pastilla de 10 mg, el farmacéutico puede dar dos pastillas de 5 mg. También pueden cambiar la forma, como dar una crema en lugar de una pomada. Además, los niños que no recibieron la vacuna contra la gripe en la escuela ahora pueden vacunarse en la farmacia.

**Impacto** – Este cambio ayuda a las personas a obtener sus medicamentos más rápido y fácilmente, sin tener que visitar de nuevo al médico para una nueva receta. También facilita que los niños reciban la vacuna contra la gripe, lo que puede proteger a más familias de enfermedades. Al permitir que los farmacéuticos hagan estos cambios de forma segura, los pacientes ahorran tiempo y evitan viajes extras.

**Próximo paso** – Las farmacias comenzarán a usar estos nuevos poderes de inmediato, y las autoridades de salud supervisarán para asegurarse de que los cambios sean seguros y útiles. Esto podría llevar a más formas en que los farmacéuticos apoyen a los pacientes en el futuro.

**Una frase clave** – Nuevas reglas permiten a los farmacéuticos cambiar medicamentos durante escasez y ofrecer vacunas contra la gripe a niños que no la recibieron en la escuela, haciendo la atención médica más rápida y sencilla.

articles.title: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time
articles.summary: Scientists have identified two potentially critical periods when screen time may be especially detrimental to children's learning and memory: infancy and the start of formal schooling. Greater screen exposure during these developmental windows was linked to poorer academic performance and weaker working memory years later.
articles.content:
Screen time at certain ages may be more closely tied to children's future learning and memory than previously recognized. A new study tracking children from age 1 to 8 found that those who spent more time watching screens during infancy and around the start of elementary school tended to perform worse academically at age 9 and have weaker working memory at age 10.5.

The findings suggest that when children use screens may be just as important as how much time they spend in front of them. Two ages in particular, 1 and 6, emerged as potentially sensitive periods in childhood development.

As digital devices become an increasingly common part of childhood, understanding their potential long-term effects has become a growing priority. Recommendations from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the American Academy of Pediatrics generally emphasize avoiding screen exposure during the first 18 to 24 months of life and limiting it to less than one hour a day for children ages 2 to 5. However, many young children spend considerably more time using screens.

Tracking Screen Time Throughout Childhood

Despite growing concerns about children's digital habits, previous research has produced mixed findings about the relationship between screen time and cognitive development. Many earlier studies examined children at a single point in time, concentrated on children already attending school, or did not regularly track screen habits throughout early childhood.

Following the same children over several years allows researchers to investigate whether screen exposure at particular ages is more strongly associated with later outcomes. This approach can also help researchers better account for the influence of family circumstances and environmental factors.

Scientists from Inserm and the National University of Singapore addressed these gaps in a study published in the World Journal of Pediatrics. The researchers examined data from 502 children participating in the Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcomes (GUSTO) birth cohort.

Parents reported their children's screen viewing habits at six different points between infancy and middle childhood. The researchers then evaluated the children's academic achievement and working memory several years later.

Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and manipulate information. It plays an essential role in everyday learning, allowing children to follow instructions, solve math problems, understand sentences, and keep track of information while completing tasks.

Two Ages Stand Out for Screen Time Risks

The researchers found that greater screen exposure at certain stages of childhood was associated with lower academic achievement and poorer working memory later in life. These relationships were particularly consistent among children who spent more time watching screens at age 1 and around age 6, when formal schooling typically begins.

Children who accumulated more screen time throughout childhood also tended to achieve lower academic scores. However, the strength of the associations varied depending on when the exposure occurred, suggesting that some developmental stages may be more sensitive than others.

One possible explanation is that screen viewing can take time away from activities that support cognitive development, including conversations with caregivers, imaginative play, and hands-on exploration of the physical world. These experiences provide opportunities for children to develop language, attention, memory, and problem-solving skills.

"The effect sizes we saw at age 1 were the largest among all time points we examined," the authors said. "That suggests early infancy may be a window of heightened sensitivity, when the developing brain is particularly vulnerable to the displacement of learning interactions by screen time. We were also surprised to see that while screen use at age 2 and 3 did not show significant links, the associations re-emerged at age 6 -- when children enter formal schooling. So it is not just about early years; screen use later in childhood still matters."

Although the study identifies associations rather than proving that screen time directly causes poorer cognitive or academic outcomes, the results highlight the potential importance of managing children's screen habits at different ages.

Why Even Small Differences in Screen Time Matter

According to the researchers, the results reinforce the principle that "less is better" when it comes to children's screen time.

An additional hour of daily screen viewing may not produce a noticeable difference in an individual child's academic abilities. However, when similar patterns occur across a large population, even relatively small differences in average performance could increase the number of children who experience academic difficulties.

The researchers suggest that efforts to encourage healthier screen habits could begin during infancy, with renewed emphasis around the transition to elementary school. This approach recognizes that children's developmental needs continue to change well beyond their toddler years.

The authors also stress that the amount of time children spend in front of screens is only one part of a much larger picture. Future studies should investigate whether the quality of digital content, the types of devices children use, and whether parents watch and interact with their children during screen time influence developmental outcomes.

Understanding these differences could eventually help researchers develop more targeted recommendations that consider not only how much screen time children get, but also when and how they engage with digital technology.

The GUSTO study was supported by the Singapore National Research Foundation and the Singapore Ministry of Health's National Medical Research Council (NMRC/TCR/004-NUS/2008 and NMRC/TCR/012-NUHS/2014). Additional funding came from the Agence Nationale de la Recherche (ANR) in France (iSCAN project, ANR-20-CE36-0001).

This knowledge has broad public health implications, informing parents, educators, and policymakers about managing children's screen exposure to improve long-term learning outcomes. The study is detailed, based on longitudinal data, and offers actionable insights for child development and health guidelines.
articles.personality_title: Study finds ages 1 and 6 are key times when screen time may affect children’s learning
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have been studying how screen time affects children’s brain development. While many studies looked at screen use at one time, this new research followed children from age 1 to 8 to see how screen habits at different ages relate to later learning and memory.

**What happened** – Researchers from Inserm and the National University of Singapore studied 502 children in the GUSTO project. Parents reported how much time their children spent watching screens at six points between infancy and middle childhood. The study found that children with more screen time at age 1 and around age 6—when kids start school—tended to do worse academically at age 9 and had weaker working memory at age 10.5.

**Impact** – This study shows that when children use screens is very important, not just how much time they spend on them. Ages 1 and 6 are sensitive times because the brain is developing fast and learning skills that need attention and memory. Screen time may take away from activities like talking, playing, and exploring, which help children learn language and problem-solving. The results suggest parents and schools should pay special attention to screen habits during these ages.

**What’s next step** – The researchers want future studies to look at the type of screen content and whether parents interact with children during screen time. Understanding these details could help create better rules about not only how long but how children use digital devices. Meanwhile, efforts to reduce screen time could start in infancy and again when children begin school to support better learning outcomes.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Screen time at ages 1 and 6 may affect children’s future learning and memory, highlighting the need to manage screen use carefully during these key developmental stages.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une étude identifie les âges 1 et 6 comme périodes clés où le temps d’écran peut affecter l’apprentissage des enfants
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Des scientifiques étudient comment le temps passé devant les écrans influence le développement du cerveau des enfants. Alors que beaucoup d’études se concentraient sur un seul moment, cette nouvelle recherche a suivi des enfants de 1 à 8 ans pour voir comment leur usage des écrans à différents âges affecte leur apprentissage et leur mémoire plus tard.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs d’Inserm et de l’Université nationale de Singapour ont étudié 502 enfants dans le projet GUSTO. Les parents ont indiqué le temps d’écran de leurs enfants à six moments entre la petite enfance et l’enfance moyenne. L’étude a montré que les enfants avec plus de temps d’écran à 1 an et vers 6 ans – âge de début de l’école – avaient de moins bons résultats scolaires à 9 ans et une mémoire de travail plus faible à 10,5 ans.

**Impact** – Cette étude montre que le moment où les enfants utilisent les écrans est très important, pas seulement la durée. Les âges 1 et 6 sont sensibles car le cerveau se développe rapidement et apprend des compétences qui demandent attention et mémoire. Le temps d’écran peut réduire les activités comme parler, jouer et explorer, qui aident à apprendre le langage et la résolution de problèmes. Ces résultats suggèrent que parents et écoles doivent surveiller particulièrement les habitudes d’écran à ces âges.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs souhaitent que les futures études examinent le type de contenu à l’écran et si les parents interagissent avec les enfants pendant ce temps. Mieux comprendre ces détails pourrait aider à créer des règles plus adaptées, non seulement sur la durée, mais aussi sur la manière d’utiliser les appareils numériques. En attendant, il serait utile de réduire le temps d’écran dès la petite enfance et à l’entrée à l’école pour soutenir un meilleur apprentissage.

**En une phrase** – Le temps d’écran à 1 et 6 ans peut influencer l’apprentissage et la mémoire futurs des enfants, soulignant l’importance de gérer soigneusement l’utilisation des écrans à ces étapes clés du développement.
articles.personality_title_es: Estudio identifica las edades 1 y 6 como momentos clave en que el tiempo frente a pantallas puede afectar el aprendizaje de niños
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Científicos han estado investigando cómo el tiempo frente a pantallas afecta el desarrollo cerebral de los niños. Mientras muchos estudios observaron el uso de pantallas en un solo momento, esta nueva investigación siguió a niños de 1 a 8 años para ver cómo sus hábitos de pantalla a diferentes edades se relacionan con su aprendizaje y memoria más adelante.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de Inserm y la Universidad Nacional de Singapur estudiaron a 502 niños en el proyecto GUSTO. Los padres informaron cuánto tiempo pasaban sus hijos frente a pantallas en seis momentos entre la infancia y la niñez media. El estudio encontró que los niños con más tiempo de pantalla a la edad de 1 y alrededor de los 6 años —cuando comienzan la escuela— tendían a tener peores resultados académicos a los 9 años y una memoria de trabajo más débil a los 10.5.

**Impacto** – Este estudio muestra que cuándo los niños usan pantallas es muy importante, no solo cuánto tiempo. Las edades 1 y 6 son momentos sensibles porque el cerebro se desarrolla rápido y aprende habilidades que necesitan atención y memoria. El tiempo frente a pantallas puede quitar tiempo a actividades como conversar, jugar y explorar, que ayudan a aprender el lenguaje y a resolver problemas. Los resultados sugieren que padres y escuelas deben prestar especial atención a los hábitos de pantalla en estas edades.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren que futuros estudios analicen el tipo de contenido en pantalla y si los padres interactúan con los niños durante ese tiempo. Comprender estos detalles podría ayudar a crear mejores reglas sobre no solo cuánto tiempo, sino cómo los niños usan los dispositivos digitales. Mientras tanto, se deberían hacer esfuerzos para reducir el tiempo frente a pantallas desde la infancia y de nuevo al comenzar la escuela para apoyar mejores resultados de aprendizaje.

**Conclusión en una frase** – El tiempo frente a pantallas a los 1 y 6 años puede afectar el aprendizaje y la memoria futura de los niños, mostrando la necesidad de manejar cuidadosamente el uso de pantallas en estas etapas clave del desarrollo.
